and 4. dhåñöa (bold and dominating). The Lord's pastime potency (lélä-çakti) manifests these various
features in the presence of the Lord's beloveds. In this way these features are seen. However, when
they are separated from the Lord, the Lord's beloveds feel great distress. In that state of calamity
they all feel friendship for each other. This is seen in the following words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.30.40):

anvicchantyo bhagavato
  märgaà gopyo 'vidüritaù
dadåçuù priya-viçleñan
  mohitäà duùkhitäà sakhém


   "WhiIe continuing to search out Kåñëa's path, the gopés discovered their unhappy friend close
by. She was bewildered by separation from Her lover."***

    In this verse the gopés' feelingsof friendship for each other is manifested. Lord Kåñëa manifests
this pastime of being separated from Him in order that the gopés' thirst to attain Him may very
quickly increase. In this way the gopés' love for Lord Kåñëa, the crest jewel of amorous heroes,
increases. That this is the true reason Lord Kåñëa arranges that His devotees be separated from Him
is confirmed by Lord Kåñëa Himself in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.32.20):


nähaà tu sakhyo bhajato 'pi jantün. . .


   "But the reason I do not immediately reciprocate the affection of living beings even when they
worship Me, O gopés, is that I want to intensify their loving devotion. They then become like a poor
man who has gained some wealth and then lost it, and who thus becomes so anxious about it that he
can think of nothing else."***

   These pastimes are the Supreme Lord's attempt to make the gopés free offalse pride. This is seen
in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.48, which was quoted above. In that verse the word {.sy 168}prasamaya"
means "to make them free of false pride", and the word "prasadaya" means "to give them mercy,
mercy that took the form of making them thirst after attaining Him". In this way the gopés' good
ofrtune (tat-subhaga) is seen. The word "prasädäya" may also be interpreted to mean "to satisfy the
gopés' passioante desires, Lord Kåñëa enjoyed the räsa dance pastime", and the word {.sy
168}prasädäya" may also be interpreted to mean "to delight the gopés, Lord Kåñëa enjoyed the räsa-
dance pastime". The word "daurätmya" here means "separated fropm Lord Kåñëa, the gopés became
depressed at heart". {.sy 168}Daurätmya" here does not mean "wickedness" because this passage
describes pastimes of transcendental love. Çréla Çyukadeva Gisvämé, the king of sages, then gave
this description in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.41):


tayä kathitam äkarëya. . .


   "She told them how Mädhava had given Her much respect, but how She then suffered dishonor
because of Her misbehavior. The gopis were extremely amazed to hear this."***

   Actually there was nothing wrong with that gopés' pride. This is seen in the following words of

Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.34):


reme tayä svätma-rata
   ätmärämo 'py akhaëòitaù
käminäà darçayan dainyaà
   stréëäà caiva durätmatäm


   "Lord Kåñëa enjoyed with that gopé although He enjoys only within, being self-satisfied and
complete in Himself. Thus by contrast He showed the wretchedness of ordinary lusty men and
hardhearted women."***

   In this verse the word "svätma-rataù" means {.sy 168}self-satisfied", "ätmärämaù" means "who
enjoys pastimes", and "apy akhaëòitaù reme" means {.sy 168}attached to that particular gopé, He
enjoyed pastimes with Her". Someone may ask: "Why was Lord Kåñëa so attached to that one gopé?
Why did He enjoy pastimes with Her?" The answer is given here in this verse, Çrémad-Bhägavatam
10.30.35. It is also said in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (1.7.10):


ittham-bhüta-guëo hariù


   "The Supreme Personality of Godhead possesses transcendental qualities."

   As the Supreme Personality of Godhead possesses transcendental qualities, so does the gopé (Çré
Rädhä) mentioned in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.30.34. Her quality is that She is filled with love for
Lord Kåñëa. Here it is specifically said that Her love is pure spiritual love. It is not material lust.
Spiritual love is very powerful and glorious. Still, this gopé's spiritual love may superfically seem like
material lust, and in this way it may manifest what seems to be material pride and material passion.
Thus this gopé reveals a kind of love that seems to be like the wretchedness (dainyam) of lusty
women, a wretchedness that is well known in this material world. Thus this gopés manifests
stubbornness, willfulness, and a personality that tries to dominate Her beloved. With this beloved
Lord Kåñëa enjoys pastimes (reme). Or, these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam may be interpreted in a
different way. They may be interpreted to mean "With these pastimes the Lord shows how
wretched and insignificant are materialistic mn who try to enjoy amorous pastimes with lusty
women in the material world. Manifesting the glory of His pastimes, the Lord shows how wretched
and devoid of true nectar are the activities (dainyam) of lusty men (käminam) and how wretched is
the nature (durätmatäm) of materialistic women (stréëäm) who do not worship the Supreme Lord."
The great glory of the gopés' pastimes with Lord Kåñëa is also seen in these words of scripture:


darçayad vidhu-paräjayaà ramä-vaktram ullasati dhüta-läïchanam


   "As the goddess of fortune enjoys pastimes with the Supreme Lord, the spotless moon of her face,

a moon that defeats all other moons, shines with bliss."

   Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.30.34 discussed in these words was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.289
records.text:
In this way the älambana of srngara-rasa has been described. Now the uddépanas will be
described. Included among the uddépanas are Lord Kåñëa's qualities, such as His ability to charm
women (näré-moahana-çélatva), The handsome charm of His bodily color, sweetness, fragrance,
touch, sound, auspicious qualities, and new youthfulness (avayava-varëa-rasa-gandha-sparça-çabda-
sal-lakñaëa-nava-yauvanänäà kamanéyatä), His being always new and fresh (nitya-nütanatva), His
making the gopés fall in love with Him (abhivyakta-bhävatva), His being controlled by His devotees'
love (prema-vaçyatva), and His genius (saubuddhya-pratibhätva). His ability to charm women is
described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.21.12):


kåñëaà nirékñya vanitotsava-rüpa-çélam. . .


    "Kåñëa's beauty and character create a festival for all women. Indeed, when the demigods' wives
flying in airplanes with their husbands catch sight of Him and hear His resonant flute-song, their
hearts are shaken by Cupid, and they become so bewildered that the flowers fall out of their hair
and their belts loosen."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the goddesslike gopés of Vraja.


Anucchedas 290-294


    Lord Kåñëa's being eternally new and fresh is described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(1.11.34):


yadyapy asau pärçva-gataù. . .


  "Although Lord Çré Kåñëa was constantly by their sides, as well as exclusively alone, His feet
appeared to them to be newer and newer. The goddess of fortune, although by nature always restless
and moving, could not quit the Lord's feet. So what woman can be detached from those feet, having
once taken shelter of them?"***

   Now Lord Kåñëa's quality of making the gopés fall in love with Him will be described. The pürva-
räga (first stages of that love) is described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.31.2):

çarad-udäçaye sädhu jäta-sat-
   sarasijodara-çré-muñä dåçä
surata-nätha te 'çulka-däsikä
   vara-da nighnato neha kim vadhaù


   "O Lord of love, in beauty Your glance excels the whorl of the finest, most perfec fly formed
lotus within the autumn pond. O bestower of benedictions, You are killing the maidservants who
have given themselves to You freely, without any price. Isn't this murder?"***

   In this verse the words "dåçä surata-nätha" mean "O Lord who with Your glance beg to
enjoyamorous pastimes", "vara-prada" means "O Lord who at the end of our worship of Goddess
Kätyäyané granted the boon we prayed to attain", "dåçä açulka-däsikä" mean {.sy 168}without giving
any money to purchase us, simply by casting Your love-filled galnce on us, You turned us into Your
slavea", and "nighnato neha kim vadhaù" mean "did You not murder us women?" In this way this
verse shows that simply with His glance Lord Kåñëa enchanted the gopés. He enchanted them in
two ways: 1. He enchanted them with His form and qualities (svarüpa), and 2. He enchanted them
with His activities others have no power to perform (duñkara-kriyä). In this verse these two ways of
enchantement are both described. Lord Kåñëa's enchanting the gopés is also described in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.31.8):


madhurayä girä valgu-väkyayä
   budha-manojïayä puñkarekñaëa
vidhi-karér imä véra muhyatér
   adhara-sédhunäpyäyayasva naù


   "O lotus-eyed one, Your sweet voice and charming words, which attract the minds of the
intelligent, are bewildering us more and more. Our dear hero, please revive Your maidservants with
the nectar of Your lips."***

   In this verse the word "madhurayä" means {.sy 168}with the sweetness of Your form", "valgu-
väkyayä" means "with the sweetness of Your words", and {.sy 168}budha-manojïayä" means "which
charm the hearts of the intelligent". In this way Lord Kåñëa's sweetness is manifest. Lord Kåñëa's
enchanting the gopés is also described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.31.10):


prahasitaà priya-prema-vékñaëaà
   viharaëaà ca te dhyäna-maìgalam
rahasi saàvido yä hådi spåçaù
   kuhaka no manaù kñobhayanti hi


  "Your smiles, Your sweet, loving glances, the intimate pastimes and confidential talks we enjoyed

with You--all these are auspicious to meditate upon, and they touch our hearts. But at the same
time, O deceiver, they very much agitate our minds."***

  In this verse the word "samvidaù" means {.sy 168}joking words".

   Lord Kåñëa's enchanting the gopés is also described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.31.12):


dina-parikñaye néla-kuntalair
   vanaruhänanaà bibhrad ävåtam
ghana-rajasvalaà darçayan muhur
   manasi naù smaram vira yacchasi


   "At the end of the day You repeatedly show us Your lotus face, covered with dark blue locks of
hair and thickly powdered with dust. Thus, O hero, You arouse lusty desires in our minds."***

   In this verse the word "muhuù" means "again and again". Lord Kåñëa's enchanting the gopés is
also described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.31.16-17):


pati-sutänvaya-bhrätå-bändhavän
   ativilaìghya te 'nty acyutagataù
gati-vidas tavodgéta-mohitäù
   kitava yoñitaù kas tyajen niçi


   "Dear Acyuta, You know very well why we have come here. Who but a cheater like You would
abandon young women who come to see Him in the middle of the night, enchanted by the loud
song of His flute? Just to see You, we have completely rejected our husbands, children, ancestors,
brothers and other relatives.***


rahasi saàvidaà håc-chayodayam
   prahasitänanaà prema-vékñaëam
brhad-uraù çriyo vékñya dhäma te
   muhur ati-spåhä muhyate manaù


   "Our minds are repeatedly bewildered as we think of the intimate conversations we had with
You in secret, feel the rise of lust in our hearts and remember Your smiling lace, Your loving
glances and Your broad chest, the resting place of the goddess of fortune. Thus we experience the
most severe hankering for You."***

  In these verses the words "gati-vidas tavodgéta-mohitäù" mean "You played on Your flute, a flute

that well knows how to bring us under its spell". These verses were spoken by the gopés to the
Supreme Personality of Godhead, who at that moment was not visible before them.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.295
records.text:
Lord Kåñëa's enchanting the gopés in the stage of pürva-räga (beginning of love) is described in
these words of Skanda Puräëa, Revä-khaëòa, Tulasé-stava:


gaväà hitäya tulasi
   gopénäà rati-hetave
våndävane tvaà väpitä
   sevita viñëunä svayam


   "To bring auspiciousness to the cows, as well as to make the gopés fall in love with Him, Lord
Viñëu personally plants You in Våndävana and serves you, O Goddess Tulasé."
   Lord Kåñëa's enhcanting the gopés while directly enjoying pastimes them is described in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.42):


iti viklavitaà täsäm. . .


   "Smiling upon hearing these despondent words from the gopis, Lord Kåñëa, the supreme master
of all masters of mystic yoga, mercifully enjoyed with them, although He is self-satisfied."***

   In this verse the word "prahasya" (smiling) describes how Lord Kåñëa enchanted the gopés.

  Lord Kåñëa enchanting the gopés as He enjoyed pastimes with them is again described in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.43, 44, and 46):


täbhiù sametäbhir udära-ceñöitaù. . .
 . . .udära-häsa-dvija-kunda-dédhatiù


   "Among the assembled gopés, the infallible Lord Kåñëa appeared just like the moon surrounded
by stars. He whose activities are so magnanimous made their faces blossom with His affectionate
glances, and His broad smiles revealed the effulgence of His jasmine-bud-like teeth.***


upagéyamänaù. . .udgäyan

  "As the gopés sang His praises, that leader of hundreds of women sang loudly in reply. He moved
among them, wearing His Varjayanté garland, beautifying the Våndävana forest.***


bähu-prasära. . .


   "Kåñëa threw His arms around the gopés and embraced them. He aroused Cupid in the beautiful
young ladies of Vraja by touching their hands, hair, thighs, belts, and breasts, by playfully
scratching them with His fingernails, and also by joking with them, glancing at them, and laughing
with them. In this way the Lord enjoyed His pastimes."***

   In this way is described Lord Kåñëa's quality of making the gopés fall in love with Him.

    Now will be considered Lord Kåñëa's quality of controlled by His devotees' love (prema-
vaçyatva). This quality is of two kinds: 1. being controlled by the love of devotees other than His
beloveds (premäntareëa), and 2. being controlled by the love of His beloveds (preyasé-premëä). The
first of these (being controlled by the love of devotees other than His beloveds) is seen in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.35.20):


narma-daù praëayiëäà vijahära


    "O sinless Yaçodä, your darling child, the son of Mahäräja Nanda, has festively enhanced His
attire with a jasmine garland, and He is now playing along the Yamunä in the company of the cows
and cowherd boys, amusing His dear companions. The gentle breeze honors Him with its soothing
fragrance of sandalwood, while the various Upadevas, standing on all sides like panegyrists, offer
their music, singing and gifts of tribute."***

   Now the second of these (being controlled by the love of His beloveds) will be considered. This
quality when manifested in the stage of pürva-räga is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.53.2):


tathäham api tac-citto
   nidräà ca na labhe niçi


   "Just as Rukmiëé's mind is fixed on Me, My mind is fixed on her. I can't even sleep at night."***

  The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the Supreme Personality of
Godhead to Rukmiëé's messenger.


Anucchedas 296 and 297

   Lord Kåñëa's being controlled by the love of His beloveds in the stage of pürva-räga is also seen
in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.1):


bhagavän api tä rätréù
   çäradotphulla-mallikaù
vékñya rantuà manaç cakre
   yoga-mäyäm upäçritah


   "Çré Kåñëa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, full in all opulences, yet upon seeing those
autumn nights scented with blossoming jasmine flowers, He turned His mind toward loving affairs.
To fulfill His purposes He employed His internal potency."***

   In this verse the word "yoga-mäyäm upäçritaù" means "taking shelter of yoga-mäyä, which fulfills
the numberless desires of numberless gopés."

   Lord Kåñëa's being controlled by the love of His beloveds as He directly enjoys pastimes with
them is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.42):


iti viklavitaà täsäà
    çrutvä yogeçvareçvaraù
prahasya sa-dayaà gopér
    ätmärämo py aréramat


   "Smiling upon hearing these despondent words from the gopis, Lord Kåñëa, the supreme master
of all masters of mystic yoga, mercifully enjoyed with them, although He is self-satisfied."***

   In this verse the word "viklavitam" means {.sy 168}the gs' appeals of love", "sadayam" means {.sy
168}merciful because He was controlled by their love", {.sy 168}ätmärämo 'pi" means "even though
He was self-satisfied, He could see the great virtue of their love for Him". The word "ätmäräma" (self-
satisfied is also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (1.7.10):

ätmärämäç ca munayaù. . .
 . . .ittham-bhüta-guëo hariù


   "All different varieties of ätmärämas [those who take pleasure in ätmä, or spirit self], especially
those established on the path of seff-realization, though freed from all kinds of material bondage,
desire to render unalloyed devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead. This means that the
Lord possesses transcendental qualities and therefore can attract everyone, including liberated
souls."*

  The two verses Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.1 and 10.29.42 were spoken by Çréla Çukadeva
Gosvämé.


Anucchedas 298 and 299


   Lord Kåñëa's being controlled by the love of His beloveds as He directly enjoys pastimes with
them is also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.23):


reme svayaà sva-ratir atra gajendra-lélaù


   "My dear King, in the water Kåñëa found Himself being splashed on all sides by the laughing
gopés, who looked at Him with love. As the demigods worshiped Him by showering flowers from
their airplanes, the self-satisfied Lord took pleasure in playing like the king of the elephants."***

    In this verse the word "sva-ratiù" means {.sy 168}Lord Kåñëa who loved (rati) the gopés (sva)".
Lord Kåñëa's being controlled by the love of His beloveds as He directly enjoys pastimes with them
is also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.20):


täsäà rati-vihäreëa


   "Seeing that the gopés were fatigued from conjugal enjoyment, my dear King, merciful Kåñëa
lovingly wiped their faces with His comforting hand."***

   This pastime is also seen in these words of Viñëu Puräëa (5.13.54):


gopé-kapola-saàçleña. . .


   "Lord Kåñëa wiped the gopés' cheeks."

   Lord Kåñëa's pastimes with the gopés are also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.33.16):


evaà pariñvaìga-karäbhimarça-
   snigdhekñaëoddama-vilasa-hasaiù
reme rameço vraja-sundarébhir
   yathärbhakaù sva-pratibimba-vibhramaù

   "In this way Lord Kåñëa, the original Lord Näräyaëa, master of the goddess of fortune, took
pleasure in the company of the young women of Vraja by embracing them, caressing them and
glancing lovingly at them as He smiled His broad, playful smiles. It was just as if a child were playing
with his own reflection."***

   Here the word "rameça" means "the controller of Goddess Lakñmé". This verse says: "by embracing
them, caressing them and glancing lovingly at them, Lord Kåñëa enjoyed pastimes with the gopés".
In this way Lord Kåñëa was controlled by the gopés' love. Here is given the example of a
childplaying with his reflection. As a child plays with his reflection, so Lord Kåñëa enjoyed pastimes
beginnign with singing and dancing with the gopés. In this activities it is seen that Lord Kåñëa and
the gopés were deeply attached to each other.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.300
records.text:
Then it is said in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.25):


evaà çaçäìkäàçu-viräjitä niçäù
    sa satya-kämo 'nuratäbalä-gaëaù
siñeva ätmany avaruddha-saurataù
    sarväù çarat-kävya-kathä-rasäçrayäh


   "Although the gopés were firmly attached to Lord Kåñëa, whose desires are always fulfilled, the
Lord was not internally affected by any mundane sex desire. Still, to perform His pastimes the Lord
took advantage of all those moonlit autumn nights, which inspire poetic descriptions of
transcendental affairs."***

    In this verse the word "evam" means "as was previously described", "anuratäbalä-gaëaù" means
{.sy 168}the gopés who loved Kåñëa eternally", "saù" means "Çré Kåñëacandra", "ätmany avaruddha-
saurataù" means "whose thoughts were filled with flirting and various amorous pastimes", "satya-
kämaù" means {.sy 168}whose love is never wrong", "çarat-kävya-kathä-rasäçrayäù" means "nectar
poems in relation to autumn", "sarväù" means "them all", and "siñeve" means "He utilized". The wird
"çarat" here may also mean "for an entire year". The word {.sy 168}çaçäìkäàçu-viräjitä" (moonlit
nights) further describes this pastime. The Lord's amorous pastimes are also seen in the following
owrds of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.60.58):


evaà saurata-samläpaiù. . .


  "And so the self-satisfied Supreme Lord of the universe enjoyedwith the goddess of fortune,
engaging her in lovers' talks and thus imitating the ways of human society."***

   This verse describes Lord Kåñëa's pastimes of joking with Rukmiëé. The word "saurata" here has
the same meaning it had in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.33.25. Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.33.25 was spoken
by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.301
records.text:
In the matter of His relationship with the gopés Lord Kåñëa Himself declares in Çrémad-
Bhägavatam (10.32.22):


na päraye 'ham. . .


  "I am not able to repay My debt for your spotless service, even within a lifetime of Brahmä. Your
connection with Me is beyond reproach. You have worshiped Me, cutting off all domestic ties,
which are difficult to break. Therefore please let your own glorious deeds be your compensation."*

   Lord Kåñëa's separation from the gopés when He went to live in a faraway place is described in
these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.46.1-4):


våñëénäà pravaro mantré
    kåñëasya dayitaù sakhä
çiñyo båhaspateù säkñäd
    uddhavo buddhi-sattamaù


    "The supremely intelligent Uddhava was the best counselor of the Våñëi dynasty, a beloved
friend of Lord Çré Kåñëa, and a direct disciple of Båhaspati.***


tam äha bhagavän preñöhaà
   bhaktam ekäntinaà kvacit
gåhétvä päëinä päëià
   prapannärti-haro hariù


  "The Supreme Lord Hari, who relieves the distress of all who surrender to Him, once took the
hand of His fully devoted, dearmost friend Uddhava and addressed him as follows.***


gacchoddhava vrajaà saumya
   pitror nau prétim ävaha
gopénäà mad-viyogädhià

   mat-sandeçair vimocaya


   "Dear gentle Uddhava, go to Vraja and give pleasure to Our parents. And also relieve the gopés,
suffering in separation from Me, by giving them My message.***


tä man-manaskä mat-präëä
   mad-arthe tyakta-daihikäù


  "The minds of those gopés are always absorbed in Me, and their very lives are ever devoted to Me.
For My sake they have abandoned everything related to their bodies."***

  This pastime is also described in the Skanda Puräëa, Prahläda-saàhitä, Dvärakä-mähätmya,
where Çrémän Uddhava tells the gopés:


bhagavän api däçarhaù
   kandarpa-çara-péòitaù
na bhuìkte na çvapiti ca
   cintayan vo hy ahar-niçam


  "Wounded by Kämadeva's arrow, Lord Kåñëa thinks of you gopés day and night. He neither eats
nor sleeps."

   Most of the princesses married by Lord Kåñëa had previously been gopés in Vraja. As time passed
in separation from Kåñëa, they became those princesses to save themselves from committing suicide
in despair. This is described in the following words of Padma Puräëa:


kaiçora gopa-kanyäs tä
   yauvane räja-kanyakäù


   "The girls who in the beginning of their youth had been gopés at the later stage of their youth
became princesses."

   That the Lord's beloveds are inclined to commit suicide rather than live without Lord Kåñëa is
seen in these words spoken by Queen Rukmiëé in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.52.43):


yarhy ambujäkña na labheya bhavat-prasädaà
   jahyäm asün vrata-kåçän çata-janmabhiù syät

  "O lotus-eyed one, if I cannot obtain Your mercy, I shall simply give up my vital force, which will
have become weak from severe penances I will perform. Then, after hundreds of lifetimes of
endeavor, I may obtain Your mercy."***

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.302
records.text:
Amongst the uddépanas is Lord Kåñëa's caste status. Lord Kåñëa's caste as a gopa is described in
these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.35.14):


vividha-gopa-caraëeñu vidagdho
   veëu-vädya urudhä. . .


   "O pious mother Yaçodä, your son, who is expert in all the arts of herding cows, has invented
many new styles of flute-playing. When He takes His flute to His bimba-red lips and sends forth the
tones of the harmonic scale in variegated melodies, Brahmä, Siva, Indra and other chief demigods
become confused upon hearing the sound. Although they are the most learned authorities, they
cannot ascertain the essence of that music, and thus they bow down their heads and hearts."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the goddesslike gopés of Vraja.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.303
records.text:
Lord Kåñëa's caste as one of the Yädavas, a kñatriya, is seen in these words of Çrémad-
Bhägavatam (10.90.20):


megha çrémäàs tvam asi dayito yädavendrasya nünam. . .


   "O revered cloud, you are indeed dear to the chief of the Yadus, who bears the mark of Çrévatsa.
Like us, you are bound to Him by love and are meditating upon Him. Your heart is distraught with
great eagerness, as our hearts are, and as you remember Him again and again you shed a torrent of
tears. Association with Kåñëa brings such misery!"***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the Lord's queens.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.304
records.text:
Now Lord Kåñëa's activities (kriyä) will be considered. The Lord's activities are of two kinds: 1.
bhäva-sambandhiné (activities of love), and 2. sväbhävika-vinodamaya (pastimes that come from

His own nature). The first of these two kinds of activities (activities of love) is described in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.4):


niçamya gétaà tad anaìga-vardhanam. . .


   "When the young women of Våndävana heard Kåñëa's flute song, which arouses romantic
feelings, their minds were captivated by the Lord. They went to where their lover waited, each
unknown to the others, moving so quickly that their earrings swung back and forth."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.305
records.text:
The second of these two kinds of activities (pastiems that come from His own nature) is
described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.35.2):


väma-bähu-kåta-väma-kapolo
  valgita-bhrur adharärpita-veëum. . .


   "When Mukunda vibrates the flute He has placed to His lips, stopping its holes with His tender
fingers, He rests His left cheek on His left arm and makes His eyebrows dance. At that time the
demigoddesses traveling in the sky with their husbands, the Siddhas, become amazed. As those
ladies listen, they are embarrassed to find their minds yielding to the pursuit of lusty desires, and in
their distress they are unaware that the belts of their garments are loosening."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the goddesslike gopés of Vraja.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.306
records.text:
These activities are also seen in the following words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.35.14):


vividha-gopa-caraëeñu. . .


   "O pious mother Yaçodä, your son, who is expert in all the arts of herding cows, has invented
many new styles of flute-playing. When He takes His flute to His bimba-red lips and sends forth the
tones of the harmonic scale in variegated melodies, Brahmä, Siva, Indra and other chief demigods
become confused upon hearing the sound. Although they are the most learned authorities, they

cannot ascertain the essence of that music, and thus they bow down their heads and hearts."***

   Now the Lord's paraphernalia (dravya) will be considered. Amongst them are the Lord's
beloveds, who are described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.22.6):


uñasy utthäya gotraiù svair
   anyonyäbaddha-bähavaù
kåñëam uccair jagur yäntyaù
   kälindyäà snätum anvaham


   "Each day they rose at dawn. Calling out to one another by name, they all held hands and loudly
sang the glories of Kåñëa while going to the Kälindé to take their bath."***

  In this verse the word "gotraiù" means {.sy 168}in various groups". This verse was spoken by Çréla
Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.307
records.text:
The Lord's beloveds are also described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.21.3):


tad vraja-striya äçrutya. . .sva-sakhébhyo 'nvavarëayan


   "When the young ladies in the cowherd village of Vraja heard the song of Kåñëa's flute, which
arouses the influence of Cupid, some of them privately began describing Kåñëa's qualities to their
intimate friends."***

   The Lord's personal associates (parikara) are described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.47.1):


taà vékñya kåñëänucaraà vraja-striyaù. . .


   "The young women of Vraja becamne astonished upon seeing Lord Kåñëa's servant, who had
long arms, whose eyes resembled a newly grown lotus, who wore a yellow garment and a lotus
garland, and whose lotuslike face glowed with brightly polished earrings. `Who is this handsome
man?', the gopés asked. `Where has he come from, and whom does he serve? He's wearing Kåñëa's
clothes and ornaments!' Saying this, the gs eagerly crowded around Uddhava, whose shelter was the
lotus feet of Lord Uttamaùçloka, Çré Kåñëa."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

Anucchedas 308 and 309


   Lord Kåñëa's ornaments (maëòana) are described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.21.17):


pürëäù pulindya urugäya-padäbja-räga-çré-kuìkumena dayitä. . .


   "The aborigine women of the Våndävana area become disturbed by lust when they see the grass
marked with reddish kuìkuma
powder. Endowed with the color of Kåñëa's lotus feet, this powder originally decorated the breasts
of His beloveds, and when the aborigine women smear it on their faces and breasts, they give up all
their anxiety."***

   Lord Kåñëa's flute is described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.21.9):


gopyaù kim äcarad ayaà kuçalaà sma veëuù. . .


   "My dear gopés, what auspicious activities must the flute have performed to enjoy the nectar of
Kåñëa's lips independently and leave only a taste for us gopés, for whom that nectar is actually
meant! The forefathers of the flute, the bamboo trees, shed tears of pleasure. His mother, the river
on whose bank the bamboo was born, feels jubilation, and therefore her blooming lotus flowers are
standing like hair on her body."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the gopés.


Anucchedas 310-312


   The auspicious marks on Lord Kåñëa's feet are described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.30.25):


padäni vyaktam etäni
  nanda-sünor mahätmanaù


   "The marks of a flag, lotus, thunderbolt, elephant goad, barleycorn and so forth on these
footprints clearly distinguish them as belonging to that great soul, the son of Nanda Mahäräja."***

   The dust from Lord Kåñëa's feet is described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.29):


dhanyä aho amé alyo
   govindäìghry-abja-reëavaù
yän brahmeçau ramä devé
   dadhur mürdhny agha-nuttaye


  "O girls! The dust of Govinda's lotus feet is so sacred that even Brahmä, Çiva and the goddess
Ramä take that dust upon their heads to dispel sinful reactions."***

   This kind of ecstatic love (prema) for Lord Kåñëa is the most exalted (utkarña) love. Love mixed
with awareness of Lord Kåñëa's power and opulence (aiçvarya-jïäna) is not the most exalted. This
most exalted love enables one to directly see the most exalted object (viñaya) of love. Mahäräja
Bharata, who had fallen in love with a deer, praised the earth's good fortune for having been
touched by the deer's hhofs. He said in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (3.8.23):


kià vä are äcaritaà tapas tapasvinyänayä yad iyam avaniù. . .


   "O unfortunate Bharata, your austerities and penances are very insignificant compared to the
penance and austerity undergone by this earth planet. Due to the earth's severe penances, the
footprints of this deer, which are small, beautiful, most auspicious, and soft are impressed on the
surface of this most fortunate planet."*

   In a similar way the earth is also praised in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.10):


kià te kåtaà kñiti tapo bata keçaväìghri-
   sparçotsavotpulakitäìga-ruhair vibhäsi
apy aìghri-sambhava urukrama-vikramäd vä
   aho varaha-vapuñaù parirambhaneëa


    "O mother earth, what austerity did you perform to attain the touch of Lord Keçava's lotus feet,
which has brought you such great joy that your bodily hairs are standing on end? You appear very
beautiful in this condition. Was it during the Lord's current appearance that you acquired this
ecstatic symptom, or was it perhaps much earlier, when He stepped upon you in His form of the
dwarf Vämanadeva, or even earlier, when He embraced you in His form of the boar
Varähadeva?"***

   In the first half of this verse the glory of Lord Kåñëa's sweetness is described. In the second half
of this verse the lesser nature of the sweetness present in the Lord's other forms is described. In this
verse the word "api" means {.sy 168}whether?" This verse asks: "Did you attain this ecstatic joy from

the touch of the Lord's feet when the Lord stepped upon you in His form of the dwarf Varähadeva?"
Here the word "aho" is used to introduce a different idea, the idea expressed in these words: "Did
you attain this ecstatic joy from the touch of the Lord's feet when He embraced you in His form of
the boar Vämanadeva?" The implied answer to these two rhetorical questions is: "Certainly not.
Certainly not." An obscure definition of the word "api" is "butter". Interpreted in this way, the
passage becomes: "filled with bliss by the touch of the Lord's feet, the earth became soft like butter".
This verse was spoken by the gopés.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.313
records.text:
The marks left by the Lord's nails is described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.13):


påcchatemä latä bähün. . .


   "Let us ask these creepers about Kåñëa. Even though they are embracing the arms of their
husband, this tree, they certainly must have been touched by Kåñëa's fingernails, since out of joy
they are manifesting eruptions on their skin."***

   Also included here are Våndävana forest, the Yamunä, and other places of Lord Kåñëa's
pastimes. Now the different times of Lord Kåñëa's räsa-dance festival and other pastimes will be
considered. The tiem of the räsa-dance pastime is described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.47.43):


täù kià niçäù smarati yäsu. . .


   "Does He recall those nights in the Våndävana forest, lovely with lotus, jasmine, and the bright
moon? As we glorified His charming pastimes, He enjoyed with us, His beloved girlfriends, in the
circle of the räsa dance, which resounded with the music of ankle bells."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear this verse was spoken by the gopés.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.314
records.text:
Thus the Lord's transcendental qualities and other features are indluded among the uddépanas.
Because the Lord's beloveds are diligently engaged in His service, the qualities of the Lord's
beloveds are also included among the uddépanas. Thus the Lord's qualities and His belovweds'
qualities are both includedamong the uddépanas. Now the anubhävas will be considered. Examples
of the anubhävas for Kubjä and other like beloveds of the Lord are seen in these words of Çrémad-

Bhägavatam (10.48.5):


sä majjanälepa-duküla-bhüñaëa-
   srag-gandha-tämbüla-sudhäsavädibhiù
prasädhitätmopasasära mädhavam


   "Trivakrä (Kubjä) prepared herself by bathing, anointing her body, and dressing in fine
garments, by putting on jewelry, garlands, and perfume, and also by chewing betelnut, drinking
fragrant liquor, and so on. She then approached Lord Mädhava with shy, playful smiles and
coquettish glances."***

  The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.315
records.text:
Examples of the anubhävas for Lord Kåñëa's queens are seen in these words of Çrémad-
Bhägavatam (10.59.44-45):


itthaà ramä-patim aväpya. . .


   "Thus those women obtained as their husband the husband of the goddess of fortune, although
even great demigods like Brahmä do not know how to approach Him. With ever-increasing pleasure
they experienced loving attraction for Him, exchanged smiling glances with Him and reciprocated
with Him in ever-fresh intimacy, replete with joking and feminine shyness.***
   "Although the Supreme Lord's queens each had hundreds of maidservants, they chose to
personally serve the Lord by approaching Him humbly, offering Him a seat, worshipping Him with
excellent paraphernalia, bathing and massaging His feet, givin Him pän to chew, fanning Him,
anointing Him with fragrant sandalwood paste, adorning Him with flower garlands, dressing His
hair, arranging His bed, bathing Him, and presenting Him with various gifts."***

  Examples of anubhävas for the goddesslike gopés of Vraja are seen in these words of Çrémad-
Bhägavatam (10.47.61):


äsäm aho. . .yä dustyajam


   "The gopés of Våndävana have given up the association of their husbands, sons, and other family
members, who are very difficult to give up, and they have forsaken the path of chastity to take
shelter of the lotus feet of Mukunda, Kåñëa, which one should search for by Vedic knowledge. Oh,

let me be fortunate enough to be one of the bushes, creepers, or herbs in Våndävana, because the
gopés trample them and bless them with the dust of their feet."***

   Examples of anubhävas for the gopés are also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.15.42-43):


taà gorajas-churita-kuntala-baddha-barha-
   vanya-prasüna-rucirekñaëa-cäru-häsam
veëum kvaëantam anugair upagéta-kértià
   gopyo didåkñita-dåço 'bhyagaman sametäù


   "Lord Kåñëa's hair, powdered with the dust raised by the cows, was decorated with a peacock
feather and forest flowers. The Lord glanced charmingly and smiled beautifully, playing upon His
flute while His companions chanted His glories. The gopés, all together, came forward to meet Him,
their eyes very eager to see Him.***


pétvä mukunda-mukha-saragham akñi-bhångais
   täpaà jahur viraha jaà vraja-yoñito 'hni
tat sat-kåtià samadhigamya viveça goñthaà
   savriòa-hasa-vinayam yad apanga-moksam


   "With their beelike eyes, the women of Våndävana drank the honey of the beautiful face of Lord
Mukunda, and thus they gave up the distress they had felt during the day because of separation
from Him. The young Våndävana ladies cast sidelong glances at the Lord-glances filled with
bashfulness, laughter and submission-and Sré Kåñëa, completely accepting these glances as a proper
offering of respect, entered the cowherd village."***

   The meaning of these verses is clear. These verses were spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.


Anucchedas 316 and 317


   The anubhävas of the Lord's beloveds are of four kinds: 1. udbhäsvara (bodily luster), 2. sättvika
(nature), 3. alaìkära (ornaments), and 4. väcika (speech). The udbhäsvara-anubhävas are described
in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 63:


névy-uttaréya-dhammilla-
   sramsanaà gätra-moöanam
jåmbhä ghräëasya phullatvaà
   niçväsädyäç ca te matäù

    "Included amongst the udbhäsvaras are: 1. loosening of the tight belt, 2. loosening of the bodice,
3. loosening of the braids, 4. crushing of the limbs, 5. yawning, 6. expansion of the notrils, and 7.
sighing."

   The udbhäsvara-anubhävas are also described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.17):


tad-aìga-saìga-pramudäkulendriyäh
   keçän dukülaà kuca-paööikäà vä
näïjaù prativyoòhum alaà vraja-striyo
   visrasta-maläbharaëäù kurüdvaha


   "Their senses overwhelmed by the joy of having His physical association, the gopés could not
prevent their hair, their dresses and the cloths covering their breasts from becoming disheveled.
Their garlands and ornaments scattered, O hero of the Kuru dynasty."***

   The sättvika-anubhävas are described in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.11):


tatraikäàsa-gataà bähuà
   kåñëasyotpala-saurabham
candanäliptam äghräya
   håñöa-romä cucumba ha


   "Upon the shoulder of one gopé Kåñëa placed His arm, whose natural blue-lotus fragrance was
mixed with that of the sandalwood pulp anointing it. As the gopé relished that fragrance, her bodily
hair stood on end in jubilation, and she kissed His arm."***

  The meaning of these verses is clear. The two Çrémad-Bhägavatam verses were spoken by Çréla
Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.318
records.text:
The alaìkära-anubhävas are 20 in number. Of these the three manifesated on the bodily limbs
(aìgaja) are: 1. bhäva, 2. häva, and 3. helä. The seven manifested wityhout any effort (ayatnaja)
include: 1. çobhä, 2. mädhurya, 3. prägalbhya, 4. audärya, 5. dhairya (the remaining two are känti
and dépti). The ten manifested from the lover's own nature are: 1. lélä, 2. viläsa, 3. vicchitti, 4.
kilakiïcita, 5. vibhrama, 6. vibboka, 7. lalita, 8. kuööamita, 9. moööayita, and 10. vikåta. Bhäva is
described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 6:

nirvikärätmake citte
   bhävaù prathama-vikriyä


   "The first stage of anubhäva is called bhäva. In that stage the external ecstatic symptoms are
absent."

   Bhäva is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.34):


cittaà sukhena bhavatäpahåtaà gåheñu. . .


  "Until today our minds were absorbed in household affairs, but You easily stole both our minds
and our hands away from our housework. Now our feet won't move one step from Your lotus feet.
How can we go back to Vraja? What would we do there?"***

   The meaning of this vrerse is clear. This verse was spoken by the gopés.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.319
records.text:
Häva is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 9:


gréva-recaka-samyukto
   bhrü-neträdi-vikäsa-kåt
bhäväd éñat-prakäço yaù
   sa häva iti kathyate


   "When there is a slight manifestation of ecstatic symptoms, when the neck becomes titled, and
the eyebrows, eyes, and other bodily features blossom with happiness, that stage is called häva."

   Häva is seen in the following words spoken by Queen Lakñmaëä describing her svayamvara
(Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.83.29):


unnéya vaktram uru-kuntala-kuëòala-tviò-
   gaëòa-sthalaà çiçira-häsa-kaöäkña-mokñaiù
räjïo nirékñya paritaù çanakair murärer
   aàse 'nurakta-hådayä nidadhe sva-mäläm


   "I lifted my face, which was encircled by abundant locks and effulgent from the glow of my

earrings reflected from my cheeks. Smiling cooly, I glanced about. Then, looking around at all the
kings, I slowly placed the necklace on the shoulder of Muräri, who had captured my heart."***

   Had this passage been in prose, the order of the words would have been: "vaktram unnéya räjïaù
parito nirékñya çiçira-häsa-kaöäkña-mokñair murärer aàse mäläà çanakair nidadhe." Here the word
"çanakaiù" (slowly) shows that her neck was, for a moment, titled out of shyness. This is an example
of tilting the neck (gréva-recaka) a manifestation of häva. This verse was spoken by Queen
Lakñmaëä.


Anucchedas 320 and 321


   Helä is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 11:


häva eva bhaved dhelä
  vyaktaù çåìgära-sücakaù


   "After häva is the stage helä, which is the harbinger of amorous pastimes."

   Çobhä is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 13:


sä çobhä rüpa-bhogädyair
   yat syäd aìga-vibhüñaëam


   "In the state called çobhä the body is decorated with various symptoms of conjugal enjoyment."

   Çobhä is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.20):


täsäà rati-vihäreëa. . .


   "Seeing that the gopés were fatigued from conjugal enjoyment, my dear King, merciful Kåñëa
lovingly wiped their faces with His comforting hand."***

   Çobhä is also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.21-22):


gopyaù sphurat-puraöa-kuëòala. . .


   "The gopés honored their hero with smiling glances sweetened by the beauty of their cheeks and

the effulgence of their curly locks and glittering golden earrings. Overjoyed from the touch of His
fingernails, they chanted the glories of His all-auspicious transcendental pastimes.***
   "Lord Kåñëa's garland had been crushed during His conjugal dalliance with the gopés and colored
vermillion by the kuìkuma powder on their breasts. To dispel the fatigue of the gopés, Kåñëa
enetred the water of the Yamunä, followed siftly by bees who were singing like the best of the
Gandharvas. He appeared like a lordly elephant entering the water to relax in the company of his
consorts. Indeed, the Lord had transgressed all worldly and Vedic morality just as a powerful
elephant might break the dikes in a paddy field."***

  Mädhurya is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 17:


mädhuryaà näma ceñöänäà
  sarvävasthäsu cärutä


  "When all activities are naturally charming and graceful, that is called mädhurya."

  Mädhurya is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.10):


käcid räsa-pariçräntä
   pärçva-sthasya gadä-bhrtah
jagräha bähunä skandhaà
   çlathad-valaya-mallikä


   "When one gopé grew tired from the räsa dance, She turned to Kåñëa, standing at Her side
holding a baton, and grasped His shoulder with Her arm. The dancing had loosened Her bracelets
and the flowers in Her hair."***

  The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.322
records.text:
Prägalbhya is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 19:


niùçaìkatvaà prayogeñu
   budhair uktä pragalbhatä


  "Complete lack of snyness in the course of amorous pastimes is called prägalbhya by the wise."

  Prägalbhya is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.33.11):

tatraikäàsa-gataà bähum. . .


   "Upon the shoulder of one gopé Kåñëa placed His arm, whose natural blue-lotus fragrance was
mixed with that of the sandalwood pulp anointing it. As the gopé relished that fragrance, her bodily
hair stood on end in jubilation, and she kissed His arm."***

   Audärya is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 20:


audäryaà vinayaà prähuù
  sarvävasthä-gataà budhäù


   "When one is always humble in all situations, this quality is called audärya by the wise."

   Audärya is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.40):


hä nätha ramaëa preñöha. . .


   "O master! My lover! O dearmost, where are You? Where are You? Please, O mighty-armed one,
O friend, show Yourself to Me, Your poor servant!"***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çré Rädhä Herself.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.323
records.text:
Audärya is also seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.47.21):


api bata madhu-puryäm. . .


   "O Uddhava! It is indeed regrettable that Kåñëa resides in Mathurä. Does He remember His
father's household affairs and His friends, the cowherd boys? O great soul! Does He ever talk about
us, His maidservants? When will He lay on our heads His aguru-scented hand? "***

   Dhairya is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 23:


sthirä cittonnatir yä tu
   tad dhairyam iti kértyate

   "When the mind is very steady, that state is called dhairya."

   Dhairya is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.47.17):


mågayur iva kapéndram. . .dustyajas tat-kathärthaù


   "Like a hunter He cruelly shot the king of the monkeys with arrows. Because He was conquered
by a woman, He disfigured another woman who came to Him with lusty desires. And even after
consuming the gifts of Bali Maharaja, He bound him up with ropes as if he were a crow. So let us
give up all friendship with this dark-compexioned boy, even if we can't give up talking about
Him."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çré Rädhä Herself.


Anucchedas 324 and 325


   Känti and Dépti are described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Texts
14 and 15:


çobhaiva käntir äkhyätä
   manmathäpyayanojjvalä


   "When beauty increases amorous desire, this stage is called känti."


käntir eva vayo-bhoga-
  deça-käla-guëädibhiù
uddépitäti-vistäraà
  präptä ced déptir ucyate


   "If beauty is greatly increased by youthfulness, amorous enjoyment, place, time, various qualities,
or other things, that condition of increased beauty is called dépti."

   Lélä is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 24:


priyänukaraëaà lélä
   ramyair veça-kriyädibhiù

   "Lélä is the imitation of the charming apperance, activities, or other things of the beloved."

   Lélä is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.1-2):


antarhite bhagavati. . .


   "When Lord Kåñëa disappeared so suddenly, the gopés felt great sorrow at losing sight of Him,
like a group of female elephants who have lost their mate."***


gatyänuräga-smita. . .


   "As the cowherd women remembered Lord Kåñëa, their hearts were overwhelmed by His
movements and loving smiles, His playful glances and enchanting talks, and by the many other
pastimes He would enjoy with them. Thus absorbed in thoughts of Kåñëa, the Lord of Ramä, the
gopés began acting out His various transcendental pastimes."***

   The pastimes the gopés had enjoyed with Kåñëa are seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.29.46):


bähu-prasära. . .


   "Kåñëa threw His arms around the gopés and embraced them. He aroused Cupid in the beautiful
young ladies of Vraja by touching their hands, hair, thighs, belts, and breasts, by playfully
scratching them with His fingernails, and also by joking with them, glancing at them, and laughing
with them. In this way the Lord enjoyed His pastimes."***

   As the gopés imitated Lord Kåñëa's pastimes in their ecstasy of lélä-anubhäva, they acted as if
they were not different from Lord Kåñëa. This is seen in the following words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam
(10.30.3):


gati-smita-prekñaëa-bhäsaëädiñu. . .


   "Because the beloved gopés were absorbed in thoughts of their beloved Kåñëa, their bodies
imitated His way of moving and smiling, His way of beholding them, His speech and His other
distinctive features. Deeply immersed in thinking of Him and maddened by remembering His
pastimes, they declared to one another, `I am Kåñna!' "***

   As they imitated Lord Kåñëa's pastimes, the gopés' original nature became concealed. This is seen
in the following words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.20):


yatanty unnidadhe 'mbaram


   " `Don't be afraid of the wind and rain,' said one gopé. `I will save you.' And with that she lifted
her shawl above her head."***

   Overcome with ecstatic love, the gopés passed the time in this way, imitating Lord Kåñëa's
pastimes. However, they did not imitate all of Lord Kåñëa's pastimes. They imitated His childhood
pastimes and some other pastimes, but they did not imitate His pastimes in çåìgara-rasa. The gs
imitated Lord Kåñëa's pastimes with Putana and other enemies and they also imitated Lord Kåñëa's
pastimes with His mother and His other loving associates. To increase their love for Lord Kåñëa,
they passed the time in separation from Him by artifically acting out His pastimes. They did not
believe that they were truly Lord Kåñëa. Here some philosophers say: "When they were
remembering the pastime of killing Pütanä, some gopés played the role of Pütanä. Even though it
was only play-acting, the other gopés became fearful for child Kåñëa's welfare. Even in the ordinary
affairs of this world an expert actor playing the role of a ferocious tiger may bring a moment's fear
to his audience. In this way, by feeling fear for Lord Kåñë's safety in the course of this play-acting,
the gopés felt their love for Lord Kåñëa increase. Also, the gopé playing the role of Pütanä did not
feel hatred for Lord Kåñëa. In these pastimes of play-acting the gopés aways felt love for Lord Kåñëa.
In these pastimes the gopés also assumed the role of Mother Yaçodä. An example of this is seen in
these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.30.23):


baddhänyayä srajä käcit. . .


  "One gopé tied up her slender companion with a flower garland and said, `Now I will bind this
boy who has broken the butter pots and stolen the butter.' The second gopé then covered her face
and beautiful eyes, pretending to be afraid."***

  In this way they meditated on Lord Kåñëa's Dämodara pastimes, pastimes described in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (1.8.31):


vaktraà ninéya bhaya-bhävanayä sthitasya. . .


   "My dear Kåñëa, Yaçodä took up a rope to bind You when You committed an offense, and Your
perturbed eyes overflooded with tears, which washed the mascara from Your eyes. And You were
afraid, though fear personified is afraid of You. This sight is bewildering to me."*

   In these words child Kåñëa's fear of Mother Yaçodä is described. The gopés imitated this pastime

and Lord Kåñëa's other childhood pastimes. One gopé, playing the part of Mother Yaçodä, tied up
another gopé, who was playing the part of child Kåñëa. As was said before, in the course of these
pastimes of play-acting the gopés always felt love for Lord Kåñëa. In these pastimes the gopés always
took dhelter of their natural love for Lord Kåñëa. Even though one gopé played the role of Mother
Yaçodä and another gopé played the role of child Kåñëa, their original love for Lord Kåñëa in
çåìgära-rasa remained unchanged. Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.30.3 quoted in this anuccheda was
spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.326
records.text:
Viläsa-anubhäva is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 27:


gati-sthänäsanädénäà
   mukha-neträdi-karmaëäm
tat-kälikaà tu vaiçiñöyaà
   viläsaù priya-saìgajam


   "The graceful gestures of the face, eyes, and other parts of the body while walking, sitting,
standing, and enjoying various pastimes with the beloved Lord Kåñëa are called viläsa."

   Viläsa is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.32.3):


taà vilokyägataà preñöhaà
   préty-utphulla-dåço 'baläù


   "When the gopés saw that their dearmost Kåñëa had returned to them, they all stood up at once,
and out of their affection for Him their eyes bloomed wide. It was as if the air of life had reentered
their bodies."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.327
records.text:
Kila-kiïcita is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 39:


garväbhiläña-rudita-
   smitäsüya-bhaya-krudham
saìkaré-karaëaà harñäd

   ucyate kila-kiïcitam


  "Pride, ambition, weeping, smiling, envy, fear, and anger are the seven ecstatic loving symptoms
manifest by a jubilant shrinking away, and these symptoms are called kila-kiïcita-bhäva."*

   Kila-kiïcita is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.22.12-15):


tasya tat kñvelitaà dåñövä
   gopyaù prema-pariplutäù. . .


   "Seeing how Kåñëa was joking with them, the gopés became fully immersed in love for Him, and
as they glanced at each other they began to laugh and joke among themselves, even in their
embarrassment. But still they did not come out of the water.***


evaà bruvati govinde. . .


  "As Sré Govinda spoke to the gopis in this way, His joking words completely captivated their
minds. Submerged up to their necks in the cold water, they began to shiver. Thus they addressed
Him as follows.***


mänayaà bhoù kåthäù. . .


   "Dear Kåñëa, don't be unfair! We know that You are the respectable son of Nanda and that You
are honored by everyone in Vraja. You are also very dear to us. Please give us back our clothes. We
are shivering in the cold water.***


çyämasundara te däsyaù. . .


   "O Çyämasundara, we are Your maidservants and must do whatever You say. But give us back our
clothing. We know what the religious principles are, and if You don't give us our clothes we will
have to tell the king. Please!"***

  The meaning of these verses is clear. These Çrémad-Bhägavatam verses were spoken by Çréla
Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.328
records.text:
Vibhrama is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 34:

Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.22.15):


vallabha-präpti-veläyäà
   madanäveça-sambhramät
vibhramo hära-mälyädi-
   bhüñä-sthäna-viparyayaù


   "Hastily preparing to meet her lover, the bewildered heroine may place her necklace, flower-
garland, and other ornaments in the wrong places. This is called vibhrama."

  Vibhrama is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.7):


vyatyasta-vasträbharaëäù
   käçcit kåñëäntikaà yayuù


  "Though their clothes and ornaments were in complete disarray, the gs rushed off to Kåñëa."***

  Vibboka is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 47:


iñöe 'pi garva-mänäbhyäà
    vibbokaù syäd anädaraù


   "Even though pleased by Lord Kåñëa's gift, the heroine may angrily and proudly pretend to
dislike it. This is called vibboka."

  Vibboka is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.32.6):


ekä bhru-kuöim äbadhya. . .


   "One gopé, beside herself with loving anger, bit her lips and stared at Him with frowning
eyebrows, as if to wound Him with her harsh glances."***

  Lalita is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 51:


vinyäsa-bhaìgir aìgänäà

   bhrü-viläsa-manoharä
sukumärä bhaved yatra
   lalitaà tad udähåtam


   "Playful, enchanting movements of the eyebrows, and graceful, delicate movements of the limbs
are called lalita."

  In this eay these features of ecstatic love should be u understood. Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.7
quoted in this anuccheda was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.329
records.text:
Moööäyita is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 42:


känta-smaraëa-värtädau
   hådi tad-bhäva-bhävataù
präkaöyam abhiläñasya
   moööäyitam udéryate


  "When the heroine remembers or hears about her lover, Kåñëa, love for Him is aroused in her
heart, and she hankers for His association. This is called moööäyita "

   Moööäyita is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.21.12):


kåñëaà nirékñya vanitotsava. . .


    "Kåñëa's beauty and character create a festival for all women. Indeed, when the demigods' wives
flying in airplanes with their husbands catch sight of Him and hear His resonant flute-song, their
hearts are shaken by Cupid, and they become so bewildered that the flowers fall out of their hair
and their belts loosen."***

   Vikåta is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 53:


hré-mänerñyädibhir yatra
   nocyate sva-vikäsitam
vyajyate ceñöayaivedaà
   vikåtaà tad vidur budhäù

   "When shyness, anger, and jealousy are not openly expressed in words, but displayed only by
action, that is known as vikåta by the wise."

  Vikåta is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.22.23):


paridhäya sva-väsäàsi
   preñöha-saìgama-sajjitäh
gåhéta-cittä no celus
   tasmin lajjäyitekñanäh


   "The gopés were addicted to associating with their beloved Kåñëa, and thus they became
captivated by Him. Thus, even after putting their clothes on they did not move. They simply
remained where they were, shyly glancing at Him."***

  The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by Çréla Çukadeva Gosvämé.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.330
records.text:
Vicchitti is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 30:


äkalpa-kalpanälpäpi
   vicchittiù känti-poña-kåt


  "Vicchitti is beautifuying the body with various ornaments."

  Kuööamita is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 44:


sthanädharädi-grahaëe
   håt-prétäv api sambhramät
bahiù krodho vyathitavat
   proktaà kuööamitaà budhaiù


   "When the border of Her sari and the cloth veiling Her face are caught, She externally appears
offended and angry, but within Her heart She is very happy. Learned scholars call this attitude
kuööamita."*

   In this way vicchitti and kuööamita are described. The vacika-anubhavas (anubhavas of speech)
will now be considered. Amongst them Aläpa is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi,
Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 73:

cäti-priyoktir äläpaù


   "Very affectionate words are called äläpa."

   Aläpa is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.40):


kä stry aìga te kala-padäyata-veëu-géta-sammohita. . .


   "Dear Kåñëa, what woman in all the three worlds wouldn't deviate from religious behavior when
bewildered by the sweet, drawn-out melody of Your flute? Your beauty makes all three worlds
auspicious. Indeed, even the cows, birds, trees and deer manifest the ecstatic symptom of bodily hair
standing on end when they see Your beautiful form."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the gopés.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.331
records.text:
Viläpa is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 75:


viläpo duùkha-jaà vacaù


   "Viläpa means `words born of suffering'."

   Viläpa is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.47.47):


paraà saukhyaà hi nairasyam. . .


   "Indeed, the greatest happiness is to renounce all desires, as even the prostitute Piìgalä has
declared. Yet even though we know this, we cannot give up our hopes of attaining Kåñëa."***

   The meaning of this verse is clear. This verse was spoken by the gopés.

records.title: Priti Sandarbha · PS.332
records.text:
Samläpa is described in these words of Ujjvala-nélamaëi, Anubhäva-prakaraëa, Text 77:

ukti-pratyukti-mad väkyaà
   samläpa iti kértyate


   "Conversation is called samläpa."

   Samläpa is seen in the conversation recounted in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.18-41.

    In this conversation Lord Kåñëa has two purposes: 1. to request the association of the contrary
gopés charmed by His flute music and other pastimes and qualities, and 2. as a joke, and also to test
their love, to reject the company of the gopés, who had come to Him in the forest to attain His
association. Here the words of the gopés also have two purposes: 1. To reject Lord Kåñëa's request
that they return home, and 2. with words filled with yearning to beg His company. Because Lord
Kåñëa and the gopés are equally expert in the art of graceful conversation, the rasa of thwir pastimes
is nourshied by these talks between them. In the beginning of this conversation (Çrémad-
Bhägavatam 10.29.18) Lord Kåñëa affirms that He and the gopés are equal. Then He tells them in
Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.


rajany eñä. . .


   "This night is quite frightening, and frightening creatures are lurking about. Return to Vraja,
slender-waisted girls. This is not a proper place for women."***

   These words, however, have a second, a hidden meaning. By interpreting the words in a
different way this verse comes to mean: "O girls, somehow you have met Me here. Please do not
now return to Vraja, for this night is quite frightening. Therefore you girls should not leave this
place. Instead, you should stay here with Me, your hero." By speaking the word {.sy 168}su-
madhyamäù" (O slender-waisted girls) Lord Kåñëa hints that He would become very unhappy if the
gopés left Him and returned to Vraja. Then Lord Kåñëa tells them: "As long as you stay with Me you
need not fear your relatives. He says in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.20):


mätaraù. . .


   "Not finding you at home, your mothers, fathers, sons, brothers and husbands are certainly
searching for you. Don't cause anxiety for your family members."***

   The hidden meaning of this verse is: "Your mothers and other relatives did not see you tonight.
Therefore they are now searching for you. However, they will not be able to come here to this
place." Thn word "puträù" (sons) in this verse means either "the sons of your brothers-in-law" or
"the sons of your co-wives". Then Lord Kåñëa tries to enliven the gopés by showing them the

beauties of His personal forest-garden. He tells them in Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.21-22):


dåñöaà vanam. . .tad yäta. . .


   "Now you have seen this Våndävana forest, full of flowers and resplendent with the light of the
full moon. You have seen the beauty of the trees, with their leaves trembling in the gentle breeze
coming from the Yamunä. So now go back to the cowherd village. Don't delay. O chaste ladies,
serve your husbands and give milk to your crying babies and calves."***

   The hidden meaning of this verse is: "The forest is very fearful. Therefore please do not be eager
to go to Vraja so soon." Or these words meay also be interpreted to mean: {.sy 168}Please don't leave
now." They may also be interpreted to mean: "Please don't faithfully serve your husbands." Here the
word "satéù" means "O best of girls". {.sy 168}Vatsä mä krandanti" may mean "the calvees are not
crying", "mä päyayata" may mean "don't feed them milk", "mä duhyata" may mean "don't feed them
with cow's milk". Here Lord Kåñëa hints: "If you truly love me, then please don't ignore My request."
Then Lord Kåñëa places this logical argument before the gopés (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.23):


atha vä. . .


   "On the other hand, perhaps you have come here out of your great love for Me, which has taken
control of your hearts. This is of course quite commendable on your part, since all living entities
possess natural affection for Me."***

   Here the word "mayi" is the same as mama". In this verse Lord Kåñëa argues: "If all living entirties
naturally love Me, then beautiful girls may also love Me, thinking of Me as their beloved." Here
someone may protest: {.sy 168}But is not wrong for women to renounce the vow of faithfully serving
their husbands?" To answer this proetst Lord Kåñëa tells the gopés (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.24):


bhartuù çuçrüñaëam. . .


   "The highest religious duty for a woman is to sincerely serve her husband, behave well toward
her husband's family and take good care of her children."***

   Here Lord Kåñëa declares: "The highest religious duty for a woman is to sincerely serve her
husband." However, Lord Kåñëa implies here: "But you girls have never been married to your so-
called husbands. Your marriage to them is only an imagination, a myth. Therefore you do no wrong
to abandon thse mythical husbands. You may think these persons aree your husbands. Still, the
words of the Småti-çästra affrim that you may indeed abandon the vow of serving such mythical
husbands." Then Lord Kåñëa tells the gopés (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.25):

duùçélo durbhago våddhaù. . .


   "Women who desire a good desfination in the next life should never abandon a husband who has
not fallen from his religious standards, even if he is obnoxious, unfortunate, old, unintelligent,
sickly or poor."***

   Here Lord Kåñëa declares: "A woman should never abandon a husband is not fallen." Here the
hidden meaning of {.sy 168}fallen" is "envious". In this sense Lord Kåñëa considers the gopés'
mythical husbands to be envious of Him, and therefore fallen. Thinking that the gopés might
consider their husbands not fallen and therefore stay with them, with these tricky words changing
the original meaning of the Smrti-sastra's words, Lord Kåñëa denies that the gopés have any
responsibility to serve their so-called husbands. Then Lord Kåñëa tells the4 gopés (Çrémad-
Bhägavatam 10.29.26):


asvargyam. . .


   "For a woman from a respectable family, petty adulterous affairs are always condemned. They bar
her from heaven, ruin her reputation and bring her difficulty and fear."***

   The hidden meaning of these words is: "A woman who stays near (upa) her husband (pati)
(aupapatyam) will not enter heaven."

    Thinking, "the gopés may worry that it will be very difficult to attain love for Me", Lord Kåñëa
tells them: {.sy 168}Please do not turn away from Me." He tells them (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.27):


çravaëät. . .


   "Transcendental love for Me arises by the devotional processes of hearing about Me, seeing My
Deity form, meditating on Me and faithfully chanting My glories. The same result is not achieved
by mere physical proximity. So please go back to your homes."***

   Here Lord Kåñëa says: "Transcendental love for Me arises by the devotional processes that begin
with hearing about Me. The same result is not achieved by mere physical proximity. So please enter
this forest grove, which is just like your own homes." That is the hidden meaning of Lord Kåñëa's
request here. The other, original, meaning is well-known in this world. In this way, in these verses,
with many joking words Lord Kåñëa refutes the idea that the gopés actions are in any way improper.
The condition the gopés attained after hearing these words of Lord Kåñëa is described in these
words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (10.29.28-30):

iti vipriyam äkarëya. . .


   "Hearing these unpleasant words spoken by Govinda, the gopés became morose. Their great
hopes were frustrated and they felt insurmountable anxiety.***
   "Their herads hanging down and their heavy, sorrowful breathing drying up their reddened lips,
the gopés scratched the ground with their toes. Tears flowed from their eyes, carrying their kajjala
and washing away the vermillion smeared on their breasts. Thus they stood, silently bearing the
burden of their unhappiness.***
   "Although Kåñëa was their beloved, and although they had abandoned all other objects of desire
for His sake, He had been speaking to hem unfavorably. Nonetheless they remained unflinching in
their attachment to Him. Stopping their crying, they wiped their eyes and began to speak, their
voices stammering with agitation."***

   These verses show that thew gopés did not understand the second, hidden, meaning of Lord
Kåñëa's previous words. Fillied with longing to associate withe Kåñëa, they considered His words
unpleasant. Thus they became morose. Hearing Lord Kåñëa's statements that had two meanings, the
gopés became anxious and bowed their faces and performed other like activities. There is no
rasäbhäsa in any of these actions. They scratched the ground with their toes and they spoek to Lord
Kåñëa.
   The gopés said to Lord Kåñëa (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.31):


maivam. . .


   "The beautiful gopés said: O all-powerful one, You should not speak in this cruel way. Do not
reject us, who have renounced all material enjoyment to render devotional service to Your lotus
feet. Reciprocate with us, O stubborn one, just as the primeval Lord, Sré Näräyaëa, reciprocates
with His devotees in their endeavors for liberation."***

   In this verse the word "mä" (don't) is used to refute Lord Kåñëa's request (that the gopés return to
their homes). Here the gopés say: "We have completely renounced our husbands, children, and all
else and become Your devotees. Please reciprocate with us." Speaking here the passage beginning
with the word "päda-mülam" (the soles of Yoru feet), the gopés chant the glories of Lord Kåñëa.
Here the wwords {.sy 168}duravagraha mä tyajäsmän" may also be divided {.sy 168}duravagraham
ätyajäsmän". Divided in the second way they mean: "You have completely rejected us". Then the
gopés give an example of acting properly by accepting one's own devotees and rejecting others. They
say: "Lord Narayana reciprocates with the sages who yearn after liberation and who have
renounced pious deeds, sense pleasures, and all else for His sake. The Lord does not reciprocate with
others." Then, quoting from scripture, the gopés speak the next verse to refute Lord Kåñëa's request.
They say (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.32):


yat paty-apatya. . .

   "Our dear Kåñëa, as an expert in religion You have advised us that the proper religious duty for
women is to faithfuIly serve their husbands, children and other relatives. We agree that this
principle is valid, but actually this service should be rendered to You. After all, O Lord, You are the
dearmost friend of all embodied souls. You are their most intimate relative and indeed their very
Self."***

   In this verse the word "sva-dharmaù" may be interpreted as "sv-adharmaù" which means "great
impiety". If this word is interpreted in that way, then the word "dharma-vidä" is employed as a joke,
to mock the so-called knower of religion described here. If this interpretation is accepted, then
these words are only a trick and the words {.sy 168}faithfully serve their husbands" come to mean
the opposite of what they seem. Interpreted in this way, these words reject the false religious
principles described here. Here the word {.sy 168}upadeça-pade" means "teacher" and "éçe tvayy
evästu" means "You are the supremely independent Lord. These words thus mean: "O Lord, you
reject these false principles of religion". Someone may ask: "O Lord, what is Your nature?" Here the
gopés answer with the word {.sy 168}preñöhaù" (dearest beloved). The gopés say: "You are the friend
of all living entities. You are the dearest beloved of all living entities." This means: "O Lord, by
associating with You, we will all attain grea auspiciousness." Then, refuting Lord Kåñëa's statement
in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.23, the gopés say (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.33):


kurvanti. . .


   "Expert transcendentalists always direct their affection toward You because they recognize You
as their true Self and eternal beloved. What use do we have for these husbands, children and
relatives of ours, who simply give us trouble? Therefore, O supreme controller, grant us Your mercy.
O lotus-eyed one, please do not cut down our long-cherished hope to have Your association."***

   This verse also has a second, a hidden meaning. The hidden meaning, attained by interpeting
the syntatical relationships of the words in the sentence in a different way, is: "O lotus-eyed Lord,
please cut intop pieces our desire, the desire that says, `We will become happy by enjoying the
pleasures of our meaterial bodies, material bodies that are alwasy so dear to us, pleasures we enjoy
with our husbands and children. Why should we be attracted to Kåñëa as our beloved? We are not
attracted to Him.' " Here the word "varadeçvara (givcer of boons) is in the vocatuve case. It is used
here sarcastically. Here the gopés say: "Please give this boon to us. Give us the boon that the
indifference we feel in our hearts toward You, the indifference that says, `Let us not always yearn to
attain You, O Kåñëa.', will be cut into pieces." Here the word {.sy 168}aravidna-netra" (O lotus-eyed
one) implies: "It is not right that a person with such beautiful lotus eyes will be so crooked and
deceitful to us". The word "sma here changes the present tense of the verb into the imperfect tense.
The word "äçäm" is the object of the sentence. In the next verse the gopés criticize Lord Kåñëa's
description of the way love for Him is attained, a description He spoke in Çrémad-Bhägavatam
10.29.27. The gopés say (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.34):

cittam. . .


  "Until today our minds were absorbed in household affairs, but You easily stole both our minds
and our hands away from our housework. Now our feet won't move one step from Your lotus feet.
How can we go back to Vraja? What would we do there?"***

   Here the gopés say: "As long as You had not stolen them away, our minds and hearts were very
happy. They were happy because they stayed at home (grhesu). The symptom of their happiness was
that our hands were engaged in household duties." Thinking of Kåñëa's addressing them as "su-
madhyamäù" (O slender-waisted girls) in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.28.19, the gopés say in this verse:
"Now our feet won't move one step from Your lotus feet. How can we go back to Vraja?" The
meaning here is: "We will not go back to Vraja. We will stay here." Then the gopés say: "What would
we do there?" In reply to Lord Kåñëas words "pratiyäta gåhän" (Please go back to your homes) in
Çrémad-Bhägavatam Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.27, the gopés speka the next verse (Çrémad-
Bhägavatam 10.29.35):


siïca. . .


   "Dear Kåñëa, please pour the nectar of Your lips upon the fire within our hearts--a fire You
ignited with Your smiling glances and the sweet song of Your flute. If You do not, we will consign
our bodies to the fire of separation from You, O friend, and thus like yogés attain to the abode of
Your lotus feet by meditation."***

   In this verse the gopés say: "beloved, please pour the nectar of Your lips upon the fire within our
hearts--a fire You ignited with Your smiling glances and the sweet song of Your flute." Then the
gopés jokingly say: "If You will not give us that nectar, then we will only stand here and lick our own
lips with desire to taste that nectar." Here the gopés hint that it is Lord Kåñëa's duty to protect
them. That the Lord protects His devotees is seen in these words of Çrémad-Bhägavatam (11.4.10):


dhatte padaà tvam avitä yadi vighna-mürdhni


  "O Lord, because You are the direct protector of Your devotee, he is able to step over the head of
whatever obstacle the demigods place before him."***

   Then the gopés say (in Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.35): {.sy 168}If You do not give us the nectar of
Your lips, we will consign our bodies to the fire of separation from You." The gopés address Kåñëa as
"sakhe" (O friend), in the vocative case, because in the past they had exchanged playful and
affectionate glances with Him. Here Lord Kåñëa may ask: {.sy 168}When We were children we
played and touched. Why have you gopés now become like strangers?" To answer this question the
gopés speak the next verse (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.36):

yarhi. . .


    "O lotus-eyed one, the goddess of fortune considers it a festive occasion whenever she touches
the soles of Your lotus feet. You are very dear to the residents of the forest, and therefore we will
also touch those lotus feet. From that time on we will be unable even to stand in the presence of
any other man, for we will have been fully satisfied by You."*

   This verse may also be interpreted to mean: "O lotus-eyed one, the birds, beasts, and other beings
in the forest all dearly love You as You enjoy Your childhood pastimes. Beasutiful girls think the
soles of Your feet are a great festival of happiness. We yearn to attain tyhe soles of Your feet. Still,
somehow we remain unable to touch them. When we played as children we enjoyed Your company.
But now we must stand before our elders and suepriors. No longer can we easily associate with You."
In this verse the word "bata" is used in the sense of doubt or worry. These words mean: {.sy 168}We
should escape from the circle of our elders and superiors." Remembering Lord Kåñëa statement (in
Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.23) "préyante mayi jantavaù" (all living entities possess natural affection
for Me), a stamenet that hints, "beautiful girls naturally love Me as their beloved", the gopés cite
Goddess Lakñmé as an example in the next verse (Çrémad-Bhägavatam 10.29.37):


çréù. . .


   "Goddess Lakñmé, whose glance is sought after by the demigods with great endeavor, has
achieved the unique position of always remaining on the chest of her Lord, Narayaëa. Still, she
desires the dust of His lotus feet, even though she has to share that dust with Tulasé-devé and
indeed with the Lord's many other servants. Similarly, we have approached the dust of Your lotus
feet for shelter."***

   In this verse the gopés say: "After attaining a place at Lord Viñëu's chest, Goddess Lakñmé still
yearns to attain to dust of Your feet in Gokula's ofrest, dust Tulasé-devé also yearns to attain. From
